title: I Let the Youth Soccer Coach Keep His Own Sideline Code

parts.text: I stood on the sideline at 9:10 a.m. with orange slices and a folding chair that sank into the wet grass. Coach Dean had printed a SIDELINE CODE: no shouting, no approaching refs, one parent voice. Then he screamed at a thirteen-year-old linesperson until the kid's voice cracked. I was thirty-eight, parent of a fullback who just wanted the orange slices. Dean looked at me. "That's coaching." I photographed the code on the fence and the timestamped video of the scream. At halftime he told my kid they were benched for "parent attitude." My kid had not spoken. The referee walked over with a yellow card for the coach. Dean laughed and said parent codes don't apply to staff. Then he pointed at me and told the ref I had been filming illegally.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: He benched my kid for a video of his own scream and called filming illegal.

social.video_title: He wrote the sideline code and then broke it — Part 1/2
social.description: Orange slices, a folding chair in wet grass, and a coach who thought yelling was a job title. Would you have kept recording?

parts.text: The rec league already allowed sideline recording. I sent the clip and the printed code to the volunteer coordinator. Dean was suspended two games and required to read the code out loud before kickoff. My kid started the next match. The oranges tasted like cold air and victory adjacent to victory. Dean coached with his hands in his pockets. I sat in the same sinking chair. I did not shout. The linesperson came back. Their voice did not crack. The fence still has the code. It now has a second copy in a plastic sleeve because the first one kept getting wet, like excuses.

social.video_title: He had to read his own code before kickoff — Part 2/2
social.description: League rules allowed the clip. The bench warmed up. Was coaching ever exempt from a fence sign?
